narration.en: Imagine building a company so powerful that millions of people carry your product in their pockets. A company that dominates the global mobile phone market. A company whose name becomes almost synonymous with mobile phones. Now imagine losing that empire… while the market itself is growing faster than ever. This isn't the story of a company that couldn't make phones. It's the story of a company that helped define the future of communication… but struggled when the future changed. This is how Nokia lost its empire.

narration.en: Nokia's story began long before smartphones existed. Founded in Finland in 1865, the company originally operated as a paper mill. Over time, Nokia expanded into different industries, including rubber, cables, and electronics. But its biggest transformation came when telecommunications became one of the most important technologies in the world. During the 1990s and early 2000s, mobile phones began changing how people communicated. Nokia was perfectly positioned to take advantage of that shift. By 2007, Nokia was the world's leading mobile phone manufacturer by shipments. But success can create a dangerous illusion. The belief that what made you successful yesterday will keep you successful tomorrow.

headline.en: From a small company to a global giant

lines_en: 2007 — Nokia leads the global mobile phone market

narration.en: Then came a turning point. In January 2007, Apple introduced the iPhone. It wasn't simply another mobile phone. It presented a different vision of what a phone could become. A large touchscreen. A software-driven experience. Later that year, Google and its partners announced Android, opening another front in the smartphone revolution. The rules of the industry were being rewritten.

elements.shot: Show a dark stage before the unveiling of a generic early touchscreen smartphone.
Cut to close-ups of fingers navigating a touchscreen.
Display a split-screen comparison between a traditional keypad phone and a touchscreen smartphone.
Transition to a software ecosystem visualization showing users, developers, apps, and devices.

narration.en: Nokia didn't ignore smartphones. That is an important distinction. The company developed advanced devices, experimented with different software platforms, and continued investing in mobile technology. But competing in a changing market requires more than recognizing that change is happening. It requires adapting quickly enough to remain relevant. Meanwhile, Apple's iOS and Google's Android were attracting developers and building increasingly influential application ecosystems. Nokia still had engineering expertise, manufacturing capabilities, and a recognizable brand. But those strengths could not automatically compensate for a weaker position in the emerging smartphone ecosystem.

lines_en: A strong product is not enough

narration.en: If you enjoy documentaries about the rise and fall of the world's biggest companies, subscribe for more stories about the decisions that build empires—and the mistakes that put them at risk.
